extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions), Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, and other stakeholders implementing Title IX
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX final rule compliance standards
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble discussion of the Department's final Title IX regulatory definitions and obligations, including what constitutes a complaint, disciplinary sanctions, and sex-based harassment, and related procedural responsibilities for recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “complaint” — oral or written
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint may be made orally or in writing; recipients may not deny a complaint because it was not submitted in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopted added flexibility in response to concerns that the 2020 signed-document requirement allowed recipients to disregard complaints on technicalities and discouraged reporting. While oral complaints may increase overall reports somewhat, the Department finds that flexibility is justified to facilitate reporting and effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate. Recipients are not granted discretion to deny complaints for lack of written form; however, employees (e.g., professors) may find it helpful to keep notes though the Department declines to require it or require training on recordkeeping (see §106.8(d)). A recipient must initiate grievance procedures consistent with §106.45 only when a written or oral report meets the standards for a “complaint” in §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligation to evaluate conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is obligated to evaluate conduct that reasonably may constitute discrimination on the basis of sex and ensure redress if it occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This obligation exists under Title IX as a condition of receiving Federal funds (see §106.31). Encouraging reporting and facilitating complaints is a critical part of effectuating Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate. The Department emphasizes recipients must address sex discrimination even without a formal complaint and must offer supportive measures where they have actual knowledge (see §106.44(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures obligation when recipient has actual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient has actual knowledge of possible sexual harassment, it is required to offer supportive measures to a complainant, with or without a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This obligation was part of the 2020 amendments and remains: offering supportive measures (see 34 CFR 106.44(a)) applies regardless of whether a formal, written complaint exists. The preamble notes oral reports can trigger this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping requirements for complaints and notifications (§106.8(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations contain specific recordkeeping requirements for each complaint of sex discrimination and each notification the Title IX Coordinator receives of information about conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although employees other than the Title IX Coordinator may be encouraged to keep notes, the Department declines to mandate that they do so or to require specific employee training on recordkeeping. The final §106.8(f) sets the formal recordkeeping obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.47 — Non-substitution of OCR judgment but accountability for noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assistant Secretary will not deem a recipient to have violated the regulations solely because the Assistant Secretary would have made a different determination than the recipient did under §106.45 (or §106.46 where applicable) based on independent weighing of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.47 conveys OCR will not substitute its judgment for the recipient's decisionmaker regarding weighing of relevant evidence. However, nothing in §106.47 prevents OCR from holding a recipient accountable for noncompliance with any provision of the final regulations, including whether a communication constitutes a complaint under §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation of grievance procedures tied to §106.2 complaint standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is required to initiate grievance procedures consistent with §106.45 only when a written or oral report meets the standards for a “complaint” in §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures recipients retain the ability to develop processes for prompt and equitable responses while preventing denial of investigations solely on procedural technicalities (e.g., lack of a signed document).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “disciplinary sanctions” — imposed only after determination under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplinary sanction is a consequence imposed on a respondent only after a determination that the respondent has violated the recipient's prohibition on sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition does not specify what consequences a recipient can or must impose or what factors must be considered; recipients retain discretion to make disciplinary decisions under their own policies and codes of conduct. The term remains “disciplinary sanctions” (not just “sanctions”) to reflect the disciplinary nature of the action. The definition applies to all recipients, including elementary and secondary schools, and the Department added “under Title IX” to the definition for clarity. The definition also contemplates that a respondent may be a third party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions — applicability clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations apply to all recipients of Federal financial assistance, including elementary schools and secondary schools; the definition of “postsecondary institution” clarifies applicability where certain provisions only apply to postsecondary institutions (e.g., §106.46).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The postsecondary definition was streamlined and retains inclusion of vocational institutions serving postsecondary students. The definitions are intended to provide clarity for recipients and do not create new extrajudicial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “sex-based harassment” — a form of sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-based harassment is explicitly stated to be a form of sex discrimination and includes sexual harassment and harassment on the bases described in §106.10 and other harassment on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopted a final definition that retains core elements proposed and provides clarity so recipients can identify discriminatory conduct. The definition is consistent with statutory text, precedent, and OCR enforcement practice, and is intended to help recipients understand their obligations. The Department rejected the position that it lacked authority to define sex-based harassment in regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered categories of sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute prohibited sex-based harassment, the sexual harassment or harassment on the bases described in §106.10 must satisfy one or more of three categories: quid pro quo, hostile environment, or specific offenses (including sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three categories modify “sexual harassment and other harassment on the basis of sex, including on the bases described in §106.10.” The Department clarified wording to change “other conduct on the basis of sex” to “other harassment on the basis of sex” to reduce confusion. Examples and case law inform the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: “On the basis of sex” requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that falls within the definition of “sex-based harassment” must be based on sex — i.e., it must be “on the basis of sex.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to statutory language, the Department clarifies that conduct not based on sex is not sex-based harassment even if offensive. “On the basis of sex” does not require the conduct be sexual in nature; it can include actions based on sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity, because these classifications depend at least in part on consideration of a person's sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and examples of covered bases (sex stereotypes, characteristics, pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX's prohibition encompasses at minimum discrimination against an individual based on sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained explicit references to these bases to align with statutory coverage and to help recipients identify harassment that depends on consideration of a person's sex. The definition applies to all recipients and allows recipients to adapt application for age and maturity differences (e.g., elementary students).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online harassment included within hostile environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of verbal, nonverbal, or physical aggression, intimidation, or hostility based on sex that occur online are within the purview of Title IX and may constitute sex-based harassment if they meet the definition's requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reiterated longstanding OCR positions that covered conduct can occur online or in person and affirmed prior guidance supporting this view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden/cost assessment and flexibility provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department projects approximately a 10 percent increase in complaints under the final regulations compared to the 2020 amendments but finds the associated costs justified by the benefits; recipients are afforded procedural flexibilities to mitigate burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considered impacts on small entities and maintained the 10 percent estimate absent data to change it. To help recipients address any increase, the final regulations permit flexibilities such as the single-investigator model and removal of the mandatory live hearing in all cases (see §§106.45(b)(2) and 106.46(f)(1)). The Department disagrees that these rules require Title IX Coordinators to police constitutionally protected speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator duties limited to conduct reasonably constituting sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX Coordinator requirements in §106.44(f) do not impose an obligation on a recipient's Title IX Coordinator to respond to any conduct or speech other than that which reasonably may constitute sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict First Amendment–protected rights. The Coordinator's role is to ensure response to covered conduct and not to monitor or police all potentially offensive speech.
